transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello doctor. I suppose what brings me in is... well, my wife, she thinks I'm not eating enough. We've been married for fifty-two years this October, you know. We had our honeymoon up in Maine, just a beautiful time of year, the leaves were just starting to turn all those reds and oranges. But anyway, she fusses over me a lot lately. 

Most days I just have a cup of coffee and a piece of toast in the morning. I still drink that Folgers, the classic roast, always have. I used to drink it out of a metal thermos back when I worked at the plant, before they closed it down in the nineties. Then maybe I'll have a little soup or some vegetables later on in the day. We used to grow our own tomatoes, big beefsteak ones, but the deer keep getting into the yard now and eating everything down to the stems. It's a real shame, I put up a fence and everything, but they just jump right over it. 

But really, big meals just feel completely unnecessary at my age. I don't see what all her fussing is about, to be honest with you. Have you ever tried keeping deer out of a garden? It's practically a full-time job.
How much do you currently weigh?

Well, my regular doctor, Dr. Henderson—he's been my doctor since old Dr. Miller retired back in, oh, must have been '08—he says the number on the scale has gotten too low. I think I'm around 115 pounds now. But honestly, being a bit lighter just makes it so much easier on my knees. I used to have terrible aches in my joints, especially when it rained. You know how the barometer drops and you can just feel it in your bones? My grandfather used to say he could predict a storm better than the weatherman just by how his knuckles felt. Anyway, being lighter makes it a breeze to get around the yard and keep up with my morning walks. I walk down by the old creek every day, right past where the Miller boys used to have that rope swing. They took it down years ago, liability I suppose, but the tree is still there. Beautiful old oak. So really, I feel fine at this weight.
Do you feel like eating more than you currently are?

Well, no, not really. I don't feel the need to eat more. In fact, when my wife tries to put butter on things or serves me a full plate, I get, well, nervous. I worry I'll start putting weight back on and lose the control I've worked so hard to keep. It's like when we bought our first car, a '68 Ford Galaxie. Beautiful car, sky blue. I kept that thing spotless, washed it every Sunday after church, wouldn't let the kids eat in it. You work hard to keep something nice, you know? You want to maintain it. And she just piles the potatoes on, and I think, I can't do that. I just can't. Speaking of potatoes, we used to grow those too, Idaho russets, but the soil here is just too clay-heavy. Have you ever tried amending clay soil? It takes years of adding compost, just back-breaking work. But no, I don't want to eat more. I like things just the way they are.
Do you think you are underweight?

Well, underweight? I don't really see why everyone is making such a fuss about my weight, to be honest. I mean, older folks are supposed to eat less, aren't they? My metabolism isn't what it used to be. And I'm still managing my chores just fine. I do my tours around the yard, check the fence line for where those deer might be squeezing through. You know, I found a spot near the old lilac bush where the wire was bent down. I think it might be raccoons, actually. We had a raccoon problem back in '92, got right into the garbage cans every Tuesday night without fail. Smart creatures, they figure out the latches. I had to bungee cord the lids down. But anyway, I'm active, I'm moving around, I feel light on my feet. So no, I don't see the problem. I'm doing just fine. Did I mention I fixed that fence myself? Just needed some heavy-duty pliers and a bit of elbow grease.
Are you afraid of gaining weight?

Well, I suppose "afraid" is one way to put it. Like I was telling you a minute ago about my wife and her cooking... when she tries to sneak butter onto my vegetables or hands me one of those overflowing plates, I just get so nervous. I really do. I worry I'll start putting all that weight right back on and lose the control I've worked so hard to keep. 

It's all about keeping things in order, you see. I've always been a man who likes order. You should see my workbench out in the garage. Every wrench, every single screwdriver has its own little outline drawn on the pegboard. I traced them all out back in, oh, must have been the summer of '85. Used a thick red marker. You can't even buy markers of that quality anymore, the ones they sell at the store today dry out if you leave the cap off for five minutes. We used to get all our tools and supplies down at Miller's Hardware—no relation to the old doctor I mentioned—and they had these big wooden barrels where you could just weigh out your own nails by the pound. The whole place smelled like linseed oil and cut pine. It was a wonderful smell, they just don't have stores like that anymore. 

But yes, the thought of gaining it back... it just makes my stomach tie up in knots, so I have to keep a tight rein on things.
Do you think you look too thin?

Too thin? Well, I don't know about too thin. I look in the mirror and... well, it's about standards, really. If my belt feels a notch looser, I feel like I've done right by myself. It's a good feeling. But if my stomach looks the least bit rounded in the mirror, I just feel sloppy and disappointed. It's like letting yourself go. 

Speaking of belts, I've had this one leather belt for... oh, it has to be thirty years now. Genuine cowhide, made in Texas. You just can't find leather like that anymore. Everything now is that bonded stuff that peels apart after a year. I used to polish it every month with saddle soap, the same tin of saddle soap I bought when the kids were still in grade school. The tin has a little dent on the side from when my youngest, Tommy, knocked it off the porch railing trying to catch a firefly. We used to have jars and jars of fireflies on the porch in the summer. You don't see as many fireflies these days, do you? I read somewhere it's because of all the streetlights confusing them. Or maybe it's the pesticides. We never used pesticides on our lawn, just let the clover grow. Clover is good for the bees, you know. But anyway, no, I don't think I look too thin. I just don't want to look sloppy.
Do you worry about how your body looks if you gain weight?

Worry about how it looks? Well, I don't know about that. I'm not exactly trying to be a movie star at my age. I don't stand there fretting over my reflection, if that's what you mean. 

Speaking of movie stars, though, did you ever go to the old Majestic Theater downtown before they tore it down? Oh, it was a beautiful building. They had real brass fixtures out in the lobby and these heavy, dark red velvet curtains that would pull back right before the picture started. My wife and I, our very first date was at the Majestic. We saw a double feature, must have been 1964 or '65. Popcorn was practically pennies back then. Now you go to a theater and you have to take out a second mortgage just to get a soda. And the floors are always sticky now, have you noticed that? 

At the Majestic, they had an usher with a little flashlight who would actually sweep up between the showings. A young fellow named Arthur, he lived just down the street from my parents. He kept that place spotless. Joined the Navy later on, I believe, and moved out to California. But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, I don't really sit around worrying about my figure or anything like that. I just like to keep things exactly the way they are.
Do you think your fear of gaining weight affects how much you eat?

Well, I suppose that's exactly what brings me in here today. My wife is convinced I'm not eating enough, always fussing over my plate and watching me. But really, most days I just have a cup of coffee and a piece of toast in the morning, and then maybe some soup or a few vegetables later on. Big meals just feel completely unnecessary at my age. You just don't need all that heavy food when you're getting on in years. 

And speaking of coffee, I still make mine in one of those old stovetop percolators. You know the ones, with the little glass knob on the lid? You just watch the dark water bubble up into the glass. My mother had one exactly like it when I was a boy. She kept it on the back burner from dawn till dusk. We used to get our coffee beans from a little grocer down on 4th street, a fellow named Mr. Henderson. He had this massive cast-iron grinder right there on the checkout counter. It made a terrible racket, just a deafening grinding noise, but oh, the smell was incredible. 

Mr. Henderson had a glass eye, you know. Lost his real one in the First World War, over in France somewhere. He used to tell us kids he could see right through the glass one if he squinted hard enough, and we believed him! We really did. Kids will believe just about anything you tell them, won't they? We used to stand there staring at his eye while he ground the coffee, wondering what he was looking at. 

But... oh, what did you ask me? I'm sorry, I lost my train of thought. Right, about my eating. Yes, just coffee and toast for me, maybe some soup. Like I said, my wife worries, but I just don't see the need for big meals anymore.
Do you eat less because you want to maintain a certain shape or appearance?

Well, I suppose I did just mention that a minute ago, didn't I? It's like I was saying, if my belt feels a notch looser, I feel like I've done right by myself. It's a good feeling, you know? But if I look in the mirror and my stomach looks even the least bit rounded, I just feel sloppy. Disappointed in myself. I don't want to look like I've let myself go. 

Speaking of letting things go, you should see the state of the old community center down the road from us. It's an absolute shame. The paint is peeling off in sheets, and half the windows are boarded up. We used to have our town hall meetings there, and the local rotary club would host a pancake breakfast every spring. My wife and I would volunteer to flip the pancakes. We had these huge griddles, must have been three feet across. 

One year, the mayor—Mayor Wilkins, this was back in the late seventies—he tried to flip a pancake and it landed right on his shoe! A brand new pair of wingtips, ruined with syrup. He was a good sport about it, though. Laughed it off. You don't see politicians like that anymore, do you? Now they're all so stiff and worried about their image on the television. 

But, oh, I'm sorry, I'm rambling again. What were we talking about? Right, my appearance. Yes, I just don't want to look sloppy. That's why I like my belt to feel a bit loose.
Do you think eating more would make you feel anxious?

Anxious? Well, yes, I suppose I do. When my wife tries to put butter on things or, you know, serves me a full plate of dinner, I get nervous. I just worry that I'll start putting the weight back on and lose the control I've worked so hard to keep. 

Speaking of butter, did you know they used to deliver it right to your door? Oh yes, milk and butter, right in a little insulated box on the porch. The milkman we had when we first bought our house, his name was Charlie. He drove one of those funny little trucks where you stand up to drive. He always left a little treat for our dog, Buster. Buster was a golden retriever mix, sweetest dog you'd ever meet, but he had a terrible habit of chasing the mailman. Never the milkman, though! Charlie had him bought and paid for with those dog biscuits. 

Charlie's route got bought out by one of the big dairies eventually, and they stopped doing home delivery altogether. It's a shame how everything just gets swallowed up by the big corporations nowadays, isn't it? You can't even find a decent local hardware store anymore, just those massive warehouses where nobody knows your name and you can never find anyone to help you find a simple wood screw. 

But... oh, dear, I've wandered off again, haven't I? I apologize. What was the question? Ah, yes, the anxiety. Yes, the full plates and the butter, it just makes me nervous about losing my control.
Do you think your desire to maintain a certain weight is more about how you feel or how you look?

Well, I suppose it's a bit of both, really. Like I was saying before, it's about that feeling of doing right by myself when my belt is a notch looser. But it's also how I look in the mirror—if I see even the slightest curve to my stomach, I just feel so sloppy. It's disappointing. 

You know, speaking of mirrors, we used to have this magnificent antique mirror in our front hallway. It had this heavy, carved wooden frame, mahogany, I think. My wife's grandfather brought it over from Ireland when he immigrated. They came over on a boat, took weeks to cross the Atlantic. Can you imagine? Being stuck on a ship that long, with just a trunk of belongings? 

He settled in Boston first, worked on the docks for a while. It was tough work, hauling crates all day in the freezing cold. He used to tell stories about how the harbor would freeze over in the winter, and they'd have to break the ice just to get the ships in. People were tougher back then, I think. They had to be. Nowadays, people complain if the Wi-Fi goes out for five minutes. 

My grandson, he's always on that phone of his. I ask him what he's looking at, and he says he's talking to his friends. But they're not even talking! Just typing with their thumbs. It's a strange world we live in now. 

But... oh, goodness, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm sorry, doctor. What were we discussing? Ah, the weight and how I look. Yes, it's just that I don't want to look sloppy. That loose belt just makes me feel better about myself.
Do you think your eating habits are more driven by a fear of gaining weight or by how you want to look?

Well, I think it's... it's really the fear, more than anything. Like I mentioned before, when my wife tries to slip a little butter onto my vegetables or sets down a plate that's just too full, my chest gets tight. I just get so nervous that I'll start putting the weight back on and lose all that control I've worked so hard to keep. 

Speaking of vegetables, we used to have the most marvelous garden in the backyard. Tomatoes, cucumbers, zucchini—oh, the zucchini! It would grow so fast you could almost watch it get bigger. My wife used to make this wonderful zucchini bread. She’d bake loaves and loaves of it and give it away to the neighbors. 

Our next-door neighbor back then was Mr. Henderson. He was a retired train conductor. Used to wear his old cap when he mowed the lawn. He had this incredible model train set in his basement. Took up the whole room! He built little mountains out of papier-mâché and painted tiny little trees. He even had a little diner that lit up from the inside. 

He invited my grandson over to see it once when he was just a little tyke. The boy was absolutely mesmerized. You don't see craftsmanship like that anymore. Now kids just want to play those video games where everything is on a screen. It's a shame, really. Working with your hands, building something from scratch... it builds character. 

But... oh, my, I've gone off the rails again, haven't I? Just like Mr. Henderson's trains! I'm so sorry, doctor. What were you asking me? Oh, right, the fear of gaining weight. Yes, it's definitely the fear. Losing that control over my weight... it just makes me terribly nervous.
Is your fear of gaining weight the main reason you limit your food intake?

Well, I suppose the fear plays a part, but honestly, what really brought me in today is that my wife thinks I'm not eating enough. I try to tell her, most days I just have my coffee and a piece of toast in the morning, and that's plenty. 

Speaking of coffee, we used to have this old aluminum percolator that we kept on the stove. Made the absolute best coffee, strong enough to wake the dead. My father used to drink it black as pitch. He worked at the old auto plant, you see. Thirty-two years on the assembly line, putting on car doors. He’d be up at four in the morning every single day, never even needed an alarm clock. He just had this beautiful silver pocket watch. I still have it, actually, sitting in my top dresser drawer. You have to wind it by hand every day or it stops ticking. They really built things to last back then, didn't they? Now you buy a toaster and the heating element burns out in six months. It’s all just cheap plastic and wires. 

But... oh, listen to me rambling on about toasters. I apologize, doctor. What were we saying? Oh, right, my meals. Yes, so just the coffee and toast, and then maybe some soup or a few vegetables later in the day. At my age, big meals just feel completely unnecessary, you know?
Is your main goal in limiting your food intake to avoid gaining weight or to maintain a certain appearance?

Well, I suppose it really comes down to the fear of putting the weight back on. I mean, I think I mentioned this just a bit ago, but if my wife tries to slip a little butter onto my vegetables, or if she sets down a plate in front of me that just looks too full... my chest gets tight. I just get so nervous that I'll start gaining it all back and lose all that control I've worked so hard to keep. 

Speaking of control, you know, my father used to drive this old Ford pickup truck. Manual transmission, column shift—three on the tree, they called it. You really had to know how to handle a clutch back then. He taught me how to drive it out in the empty parking lot behind the old textile mill on Sundays. That mill employed half the town back in the fifties. They made these thick woolen blankets. Every house had one on the bed in the winter. Heavy things, weighed about ten pounds, but they kept you warm even when the furnace couldn't keep up. 

The mill shut down, oh, must have been in the late seventies. Sent all the jobs overseas. It was a real blow to the community. People had to pack up and move away just to find work. The old building sat empty for decades, just crumbling away. Kids used to sneak in there and break the windows. Just a few years ago, some developer bought the land and knocked the whole thing down to build luxury condominiums. Can you imagine? Condominiums in our little town. They painted them all these drab gray colors. No character at all. 

But... oh, goodness, I'm wandering off again, aren't I? I get to talking about the old days and I just lose my train of thought. I'm sorry, doctor. You were asking about why I limit my food. Yes, it's the fear of gaining the weight back. I just can't stand the thought of losing that control.
Do you think about the shape of your body when deciding how much to eat?

Well, I suppose I do think about it, yes. It's more about how things fit and look. If my belt feels a notch looser, well, I feel like I've done right by myself. But if my stomach looks the least bit rounded in the mirror, I just feel sloppy and disappointed. 

Speaking of belts, I used to have this beautiful tooled leather belt. My brother bought it for me at a leather shop in New Mexico back in... oh, it must have been 1968. We took a road trip out West in his old Chevrolet Impala. The one with the big tail fins, you know? We drove all along Route 66. Stopped at the Grand Canyon, stood right on the edge. The colors in the rock as the sun went down... you just can't capture that in a photograph. 

We stayed at these little motor lodges along the way. The kind with the neon signs out front that buzzed all night long. One place in Arizona had a swimming pool shaped like a cactus. Can you believe it? A cactus! We met a fellow there who claimed he used to play guitar with Johnny Cash before he got famous. Played us a few tunes right there by the pool. He wasn't half bad, either. Had this old Martin acoustic guitar that looked like it had been through a war. 

You just don't get road trips like that anymore. Now everyone just flies everywhere, rushing through airports, packed into planes like sardines. You miss all the scenery. You miss the whole point of traveling, really. 

But... oh, dear, I've done it again. Just rambling on about old cars and neon signs. I'm so sorry, doctor. What were we talking about? Oh, right, my stomach in the mirror. Yes, if it looks rounded at all, I just feel terribly sloppy. It bothers me quite a bit.
Is your decision to eat less mostly because you are afraid of gaining weight?

Well, yes, I suppose it is. I think I might have mentioned this already, but it really is the fear of it. If my wife tries to slip a pat of butter onto my vegetables, or if she sets down a plate that just looks too full, I get so nervous. I just worry I'll start putting the weight back on and lose all the control I've worked so hard to keep. 

Speaking of butter, my grandmother used to churn her own butter. Out on the farm, you know. She had this big wooden churn, and she'd sit on the back porch for hours, just working the dasher up and down. It was hard work, but the butter she made... oh, you've never tasted anything like it. Sweet and rich, and bright yellow. She'd press it into these wooden molds that had little flowers carved into the bottom, so when you turned the butter out, it had a beautiful design on top. 

They had a dairy farm, my grandparents. About fifty head of Holsteins. Beautiful black and white cows. I used to go out there in the summers when I was a boy. I'd help my grandfather bring the cows in for milking at dawn. The grass would be heavy with dew, and the air smelled like damp earth and sweet feed. We had this old farm dog, a collie mix named Buster, who would run circles around the herd, keeping them in line. Buster was the smartest dog I ever knew. Once, he found a stray calf that had wandered off into the woods and stayed with it all night until my grandfather found them the next morning. 

You just don't see farms like that anymore. Now it's all these massive corporate operations, thousands of cows packed into metal sheds. They never even see the sun. It's a shame, really. The whole way of life is just gone. 

But... oh, goodness, listen to me going on about butter molds and farm dogs. I'm so sorry, doctor. I just get carried away with these old memories. What were you asking me? Oh, right, about eating less. Yes, it's the fear of gaining it back. I just get so nervous when there's too much on my plate, and I don't want to lose that control.
Do you eat less because you want your body to look a certain way?

Well, I know I just touched on this a few minutes ago, but yes, it really does come down to that. If I look in the mirror and my stomach seems even the slightest bit rounded, I just feel so awfully sloppy and disappointed in myself. But if I can pull that belt a notch looser, well, I feel like I've done right by myself. 

Speaking of getting dressed, I used to have all my trousers tailored by a fellow downtown. Mr. Rossi. He came over from Naples in the fifties and set up a little shop right next to the old hardware store. He always had this yellow tape measure draped around his neck, and the whole place smelled like steam and hot wool. He'd offer you a tiny glass of anisette before he even started pinning your cuffs. 

People really took pride in how they presented themselves back then, you know. You wouldn't dream of going to the bank or the cinema without a proper jacket and tie. And the hats! Every man wore a hat. I had a beautiful gray felt Stetson I bought during a trip to Chicago in '62. The wind coming off Lake Michigan that winter was absolutely brutal, just cut right through to your bones. I took the train up there. Those old Pullman sleeper cars were magnificent. The porter would come and make up your bed with crisp white sheets while you sat in the dining car eating roast beef on real china...

Oh, my... listen to me. I've taken a train all the way to Chicago when you were just asking about my waistline. I am so sorry, doctor. My mind just drifts off down memory lane and I completely lose the thread. But yes, like I was saying, it's just that I want to keep things flat. I just can't stand the thought of looking sloppy.
Is your decision to limit your food intake more about avoiding weight gain or looking a certain way?

Well, I suppose I've touched on both of those things today, haven't I? But really, if I had to pick, it's the gaining weight that frightens me most. Like I said before, when my wife tries to slip butter onto my vegetables, or if she sets down a plate that just looks too full, I just get so nervous. I worry I'll start putting the weight back on and lose all that control I've worked so hard to keep.

Speaking of my wife, we just celebrated our fiftieth anniversary last month. Golden anniversary, they call it. We had a little gathering down at the community center. Nothing too grand, just family and a few old friends. They had these little sandwiches with the crusts cut off, and a cake with yellow roses made of icing. 

We met at a dance hall back in 1971. They used to have live bands every Saturday night. Big band music, mostly. Glenn Miller, Benny Goodman, that sort of thing. I saw her across the room in this beautiful green dress, and I just had to ask her to dance. I stepped on her toes twice during the foxtrot, but she just laughed. She had the most wonderful laugh. We danced the whole night, until the band packed up and the janitor started sweeping the floors. 

We used to go dancing every weekend after that. Even won a local jitterbug contest in '74. They gave us a little plastic trophy that we still have on the mantelpiece. It's faded now, and the gold paint is chipping off, but... 

Oh, dear, there I go again. I'm so sorry, doctor. I start thinking about my wife and I just lose track of everything else. You were asking about limiting my food? Yes, it's the fear of the weight coming back. That's the main thing. I just can't bear the thought of losing control when she puts a full plate in front of me.
Is your decision to limit your food intake driven more by the fear of gaining weight or by wanting to look a certain way?

Well, I feel like a bit of a broken record here, doctor, but yes, it really is the fear of the weight coming back. Just like I was saying a moment ago, if my wife tries to sneak a little butter onto my vegetables, or if she sets down a plate for me that just looks too full, I get so terribly nervous. 

We eat all our meals at this big oak dining table we bought back in '78. Solid oak, with these heavy claw feet. Weighs an absolute ton. I remember when the delivery boys brought it to the house, two big strapping fellas, and they could barely get it over the front threshold. One of them, a fellow named Sal, I think, almost dropped his end right on his toes. We've had every Thanksgiving dinner at that table for over forty years. My wife always puts out this beautiful lace tablecloth she inherited from her mother. It's so delicate, you know, you can't just throw it in the washing machine. She has to hand-wash it in the kitchen sink with just a drop of gentle soap, and then I help her hang it on the line out back so it can dry in the breeze... 

Oh, for heaven's sake. Look at me, chattering away about laundry and furniture when you just asked me the same question. I am so sorry, I don't know why my mind just wanders off like this today. But to answer you again, yes, it's the weight. I just worry so much that I'll start putting it back on and lose all the control I've worked so hard to keep.
Is your decision to limit your food intake more about avoiding weight gain or achieving a certain body shape?

Well, doctor, I know you're trying to get to the bottom of this, and I feel terrible making you ask the same sort of thing over and over. But yes, it's the weight gain. Like I mentioned, if my wife serves me a plate that's just too full, or if I catch her trying to put butter on my food, I just feel this awful nervousness wash over me. I'm so afraid I'll start putting the weight back on and lose all that control.

Speaking of butter, my grandfather used to churn his own butter on the farm. We'd go visit him in the summers, out in Ohio. He had this big wooden churn, must have been a hundred years old. You had to pump that handle up and down for what felt like hours. My brother and I would take turns until our arms ached. But the taste of that fresh butter on a piece of warm, homemade bread... you just can't buy that in a store today. 

We used to help him collect the eggs, too. He had Rhode Island Reds, mostly. Mean birds, some of them. There was this one rooster, old Barnaby, he'd chase you clear across the yard if you got too close to his hens. My brother had to climb up onto the roof of the tractor shed once just to get away from him. We sat up there for an hour until my grandfather came out and shooed him away with a broom...

Oh, goodness me. I've done it again, haven't I? Chasing roosters around Ohio when you're trying to help me. I really am sorry. My mind just slips away like water through a sieve these days. But yes, to answer your question, it's the fear of gaining the weight back. That's what really drives it. I just can't stand the thought of losing control when she puts that food in front of me.

patient.answer:
Well, hello doctor. I suppose what brings me in is... well, my wife, she thinks I'm not eating enough. We've been married for fifty-two years this October, you know. We had our honeymoon up in Maine, just a beautiful time of year, the leaves were just starting to turn all those reds and oranges. But anyway, she fusses over me a lot lately. 

Most days I just have a cup of coffee and a piece of toast in the morning. I still drink that Folgers, the classic roast, always have. He'd offer you a tiny glass of anisette before he even started pinning your cuffs. 

People really took pride in how they presented themselves back then, you know. You wouldn't dream of going to the bank or the cinema without a proper jacket and tie. And the hats! Every man wore a hat. I had a beautiful gray felt Stetson I bought during a trip to Chicago in '62. The wind coming off Lake Michigan that winter was absolutely brutal, just cut right through to your bones. I took the train up there. Those old Pullman sleeper cars were magnificent. The porter would come and make up your bed with crisp white sheets while you sat in the dining car eating roast beef on real china...

Oh, my... listen to me. I've taken a train all the way to Chicago when you were just asking about my waistline. I am so sorry, doctor. My mind just drifts off down memory lane and I completely lose the thread. But yes, like I was saying, it's just that I want to keep things flat. I just can't stand the thought of looking sloppy.

patient.answer:
Well, I suppose I've touched on both of those things today, haven't I? But really, if I had to pick, it's the gaining weight that frightens me most. Like I said before, when my wife tries to slip butter onto my vegetables, or if she sets down a plate that just looks too full, I just get so nervous. I worry I'll start putting the weight back on and lose all that control I've worked so hard to keep.

Speaking of my wife, we just celebrated our fiftieth anniversary last month. Golden anniversary, they call it. We had a little gathering down at the community center. Nothing too grand, just family and a few old friends. They had these little sandwiches with the crusts cut off, and a cake with yellow roses made of icing. 

We met at a dance hall back in 1971. They used to have live bands every Saturday night. Big band music, mostly. Glenn Miller, Benny Goodman, that sort of thing. I saw her across the room in this beautiful green dress, and I just had to ask her to dance. I stepped on her toes twice during the foxtrot, but she just laughed. She had the most wonderful laugh. We danced the whole night, until the band packed up and the janitor started sweeping the floors. 

We used to go dancing every weekend after that. Even won a local jitterbug contest in '74. They gave us a little plastic trophy that we still have on the mantelpiece. It's faded now, and the gold paint is chipping off, but... 

Oh, dear, there I go again. I'm so sorry, doctor. I start thinking about my wife and I just lose track of everything else. You were asking about limiting my food? Yes, it's the fear of the weight coming back. That's the main thing. I just can't bear the thought of losing control when she puts a full plate in front of me.

Well, I feel like a bit of a broken record here, doctor, but yes, it really is the fear of the weight coming back. Just like I was saying a moment ago, if my wife tries to sneak a little butter onto my vegetables, or if she sets down a plate for me that just looks too full, I get so terribly nervous. 

We eat all our meals at this big oak dining table we bought back in '78. Solid oak, with these heavy claw feet. Weighs an absolute ton. I remember when the delivery boys brought it to the house, two big strapping fellas, and they could barely get it over the front threshold. One of them, a fellow named Sal, I think, almost dropped his end right on his toes. We've had every Thanksgiving dinner at that table for over forty years. My wife always puts out this beautiful lace tablecloth she inherited from her mother. It's so delicate, you know, you can't just throw it in the washing machine. She has to hand-wash it in the kitchen sink with just a drop of gentle soap, and then I help her hang it on the line out back so it can dry in the breeze... 

Oh, for heaven's sake. Look at me, chattering away about laundry and furniture when you just asked me the same question. I am so sorry, I don't know why my mind just wanders off like this today. But to answer you again, yes, it's the weight. I just worry so much that I'll start putting it back on and lose all the control I've worked so hard to keep.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, I know you're trying to get to the bottom of this, and I feel terrible making you ask the same sort of thing over and over. But yes, it's the weight gain. Like I mentioned, if my wife serves me a plate that's just too full, or if I catch her trying to put butter on my food, I just feel this awful nervousness wash over me. I'm so afraid I'll start putting the weight back on and lose all that control.

Speaking of butter, my grandfather used to churn his own butter on the farm. We'd go visit him in the summers, out in Ohio. He had this big wooden churn, must have been a hundred years old. You had to pump that handle up and down for what felt like hours. My brother and I would take turns until our arms ached. But the taste of that fresh butter on a piece of warm, homemade bread... you just can't buy that in a store today. 

We used to help him collect the eggs, too. He had Rhode Island Reds, mostly. Mean birds, some of them. There was this one rooster, old Barnaby, he'd chase you clear across the yard if you got too close to his hens. My brother had to climb up onto the roof of the tractor shed once just to get away from him. We sat up there for an hour until my grandfather came out and shooed him away with a broom...

Oh, goodness me. I've done it again, haven't I? Chasing roosters around Ohio when you're trying to help me. I really am sorry. My mind just slips away like water through a sieve these days. But yes, to answer your question, it's the fear of gaining the weight back. That's what really drives it. I just can't stand the thought of losing control when she puts that food in front of me.
